title: Quality planning
blurb: Define quality planning: turning the defined scope into acceptance criteria, standards, responsibilities and quality activities.
question: Before work starts on a school's new IT suite, the project manager agrees with teachers exactly what each deliverable must achieve to be accepted, which standards apply, and who will test and sign off each item. Which quality process is this, and what is its main output?

teach.h: Deciding what 'good' looks like before the work starts
teach.body: Quality planning takes the defined scope and specifies the acceptance criteria used to validate that the outputs are fit for purpose. It also sets the standards, methods, responsibilities and quality activities (such as reviews and tests) that will be used, usually recorded in a quality management plan. In plain English: before anyone builds anything, agree how you will know each output is good enough, and how and by whom that will be checked.

teach.h: Acceptance criteria are the heart of it
teach.body: Acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions an output must satisfy before it is accepted. They turn vague hopes ('a good IT suite') into clear tests ('every PC reaches the login screen within 60 seconds'). Agreed with the users and sponsor, they remove arguments at handover. Later, quality control inspects and tests the outputs against exactly these criteria. No criteria means nothing objective to check against.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Northgate School IT suite
head: Deliverable
Acceptance criterion
How checked
rows: Screen reader works on all PCs
teach.caption: Each criterion is specific and checkable, and the 'how checked' column becomes the quality control activity.

teach.body: The project manager ran quality planning during definition, before any equipment was ordered. Teachers agreed the criteria, the school's IT technician was named to run the tests, the deputy head was named to sign off, and the relevant accessibility standard was written in. When the supplier installed the suite, nobody argued about whether it was 'good enough': each item either met its written criterion or it did not.

teach.h: What the quality management plan covers

root.label: Quality management plan
root.sub: the main output of quality planning

rows.label: Example
values: Suite in use for spring term

teach.caption: Do not swap them: acceptance criteria apply to outputs; success criteria judge the whole project.

teach.text: Quality planning SETS the criteria; it does not check outputs against them. 'Inspecting finished deliverables for defects' is quality control, and 'checking the agreed processes are followed' is quality assurance. If the stem says before the work, agreeing criteria, standards or who checks, the answer is quality planning.

teach.h: Planning, assurance and control side by side

items: Quality planning takes the defined scope and specifies the acceptance criteria used to validate that outputs are fit for purpose.
It also sets standards, methods, responsibilities and quality activities (reviews, tests).
Its main output is usually a quality management plan.
It happens early, before deployment, and is revisited if scope changes.
Quality control later checks outputs against the criteria that planning set.

summary: You can now define quality planning as turning the defined scope into acceptance criteria, standards, methods, responsibilities and quality activities, recorded in a quality management plan. You can also tell it apart from quality assurance and quality control.

A.q: Which of the following best defines quality planning?
options: Inspecting outputs to detect any defects
Checking that agreed processes are followed
Reviewing lessons once the project closes
A.why: Quality planning takes the defined scope and specifies the acceptance criteria used to validate that outputs are fit for purpose.

whyNot.0: Inspecting outputs for defects is quality control.
whyNot.2: Checking agreed processes are followed is quality assurance.
whyNot.3: Reviewing lessons at closure is a post-project review.

A.q: What does quality planning take as its starting point?
A.why: Quality planning takes the defined scope and specifies acceptance criteria for the outputs within it.

whyNot.1: Lessons can inform planning, but the starting point is the scope being delivered.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks; it does not say which outputs need criteria.
whyNot.3: A final invoice comes at the end of a contract, long after quality planning.

A.q: Where are the results of quality planning usually recorded?
A.why: Acceptance criteria, standards, methods, responsibilities and quality activities are usually recorded in a quality management plan.

whyNot.0: The issue log records problems that have arisen, not planned quality arrangements.
whyNot.1: A benefits review plan sets out how benefits will be measured, not output criteria.
whyNot.3: Configuration records track items and versions, not the quality arrangements.

B.q: What is the main purpose of acceptance criteria?
options: To justify the investment in the project
To decide who sits on the governance board
To record each change to the configuration items
To validate that outputs are fit for purpose
B.why: Acceptance criteria are the conditions used to validate that each output is fit for purpose before it is accepted.

whyNot.0: Justifying the investment is the job of the business case.
whyNot.1: Board membership is a governance decision, not an acceptance criterion.
whyNot.2: Recording changes to items is configuration management.

B.q: Before building starts, a project manager agrees with users that each new classroom must reach a set temperature within 20 minutes and pass a fire-safety inspection. Which process is this part of?
B.why: Agreeing measurable acceptance criteria before the work starts is quality planning.

whyNot.0: Quality control would carry out the temperature and fire checks later, against these criteria.
whyNot.2: Quality assurance checks that agreed processes are followed during the work.
whyNot.3: A benefits review checks whether benefits were realised, usually after closure.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following would typically be specified during quality planning?
1. Acceptance criteria
2. Quality standards to follow
3. Who carries out reviews and tests
4. The results of final inspections
B.why: Quality planning specifies acceptance criteria, standards and responsibilities. Inspection results come later, from quality control.

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: inspection results come from quality control, after planning.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: results cannot be specified in advance.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong, and acceptance criteria (1) are the core of quality planning.

C.q: Which statement correctly contrasts quality planning with quality control?
options: Planning tests outputs; control sets the criteria
Planning sets criteria; control checks outputs
Both inspect outputs, just at different times
Planning audits processes; control sets standards
C.why: Quality planning sets the acceptance criteria; quality control inspects and tests outputs against them.

whyNot.0: This reverses the two: planning sets criteria and control tests outputs.
whyNot.2: Planning does not inspect outputs; it decides how they will be checked.
whyNot.3: Auditing processes is assurance, and setting standards is planning, not control.

C.q: At handover, a client and supplier cannot agree whether a new app is acceptable, because nobody wrote down what 'acceptable' meant. Which activity was missed?
C.why: Quality planning should have specified the acceptance criteria, giving both sides an objective test at handover.

whyNot.0: Quality control can only check against criteria; here there were none to check against.
whyNot.1: A benefits review looks at benefits after closure, not whether an output is acceptable.
whyNot.3: Escalating the dispute treats the symptom; the root cause is missing acceptance criteria.

C.q: How do acceptance criteria differ from success criteria?
options: Acceptance criteria judge the whole project
They are identical terms for the same thing
Success criteria are set only at handover
Acceptance criteria apply to the outputs
C.why: Acceptance criteria apply to individual outputs; success criteria are the measures by which the whole project's success is judged.

whyNot.0: It is success criteria that judge the whole project.
whyNot.1: They differ: one applies to outputs, the other to the project as a whole.
whyNot.2: Success criteria are agreed at the start and used throughout, not set at handover.

reteach.title: Think of planning a kitchen extension
reteach.question: You are about to have a kitchen extension built. What should you agree with the builder before the first brick is laid, so there is no argument at the end?

blocks.h: Agree the tests before the build
blocks.body: You agree that the extension must be watertight, meet building regulations, have underfloor heating that reaches 21°C, and have doors matching the existing house. You agree that building control will inspect the foundations, the builder will pressure-test the heating, and you will do the final walk-round and sign off. That is quality planning: criteria, standards, responsibilities and checks, all agreed up front.

blocks.text: Writing the list is quality planning. Actually running the tests against it later is quality control.

explain.body: Quality planning begins with the defined scope: you can only set acceptance criteria once you know which outputs the project will deliver.

test.q: Why does quality planning need the scope to be defined first?
options: Criteria are set for the outputs in scope
Scope must first be signed off by auditors
Scope sets the date of each decision gate
test.why: Acceptance criteria are written for the outputs, so the outputs in scope must be known first.

whyNot.1: Auditors do not sign off scope; the sponsor or governance board approves it.
whyNot.2: Gate dates come from the schedule and governance, not from the scope.
whyNot.3: Quality planning builds on scope definition; it does not replace it.

explain.body: Acceptance criteria are specific, measurable conditions an output must meet to be accepted. Good ones are clear enough that two people would reach the same verdict.

test.q: Which of the following is the best example of an acceptance criterion?
options: The project will finish by 31 March
The sponsor will chair the board meetings
Each door must pass a 30-minute fire test
The team will use a weekly status report
test.why: An acceptance criterion is a measurable condition an output must meet to be accepted.

whyNot.0: A finish date is a schedule target, not a condition on an output.
whyNot.1: Who chairs the board is a governance arrangement.
whyNot.3: A weekly report is a communication arrangement, not a test of an output.

explain.body: Beyond criteria, quality planning names the standards to follow, the methods to use, who reviews, tests and signs off, and which quality activities (reviews, tests, inspections) will happen and when.

test.q: During quality planning, a team names who will review designs and who will sign off each deliverable. Which element of quality planning is this?
test.why: Naming who reviews and who signs off sets the quality responsibilities.

whyNot.0: Acceptance criteria are the conditions outputs must meet, not who checks them.
whyNot.2: Standards are the external or internal rules to follow, not people's roles.
whyNot.3: Continuous improvement uses lessons to improve processes; it is not about assigning roles.

explain.body: The decisions from quality planning are usually written into a quality management plan. It becomes the reference for assurance and control during deployment.

test.q: Which document usually records a project's acceptance criteria, standards and quality activities?
test.why: The output of quality planning is usually a quality management plan.

whyNot.0: A benefits management plan covers how benefits will be realised and measured.
whyNot.1: A communication plan covers who receives what information, when and how.
whyNot.2: A stakeholder register records stakeholders and their interests.
